senses: Sour or curdled milk.
Wet clay or mud.
ety: Shortening of bonny clabber, from Irish bainne clábar (“mud, thick milk for churning”) or a Scots Gaelic cognate thereof; the latter is probably related to láib (“dirt, mud, filth”).
examples: Even butter had proved beyond her means, for the milk she had tried to churn had never firmed up beyond the consistency of runny clabber.

senses: Any of many marine amoeboid protozoa, of subclass Radiolaria, having filamentous pseudopodia; they have intricate silica skeletons.
ety: From Translingual Radiolaria + English -an.
examples: Water wells inkblack in the streets repeating the polelamps in glozy rosettes that dish and slide in the wash like radiolarians pale with phosphorous on a midnight sea.

senses: Having the qualities of mucus; resembling mucus.
ety: By surface analysis, muc(o)- + -oid.
examples: The virgin is released from the mucoid swamp by a water-nymph from under “the glassy cool, translucent wave,” an Apollonian realm of purity, clarity, and vision.

senses: A young actress with a promising career ahead of her.
An accomplished and important supporting player in a sports team.
A small star.
ety: From star + -let.
examples: There were other flapper-era starlets, of course—Louise Brooks, Greta Garbo—but they were poseurs by comparison.
As I saw the love-light beam From her radiant eyes, more glorious far Than the starlet's nightly gleam :
The shimmering, shivering, trembling, twinkling starlet white, Dancy rays darteth down, showering blossoms of silvern light ;

senses: A traditional South Asian preparation made from the leaves and flowers of the cannabis plant, consumed in food or drink.
Cannabis or its preparations generally.
ety: Transliteration of Hindustani بھانگ / भाँग (bhāṅg).
examples: Stramonium seed, mixed with wine, produces, according to a seventeenth century erotologist, libidinous activity. The effects, the write asserts, are similar to those produced by bhang.
He rolled out from under Zelikman, who looked surprised as if by the turn his bhang dream had taken.
Government-approved bhang shops thrive next to sweet shops flaunting rows of local desserts inside brightly lit, glass-panelled counters.

senses: Somewhat flat, in any comparable sense of the word.
ety: From flat + -ish.
examples: The hills in that part of Spain are of a queer formation, horseshoe-shaped with flattish tops and very steep sides running down into immense ravines.
The cobby cat is a solidly built animal with short, thick legs, broad shoulders and rump, and a short, rounded head with a flattish face.

senses: An interval of three whole tones.
ety: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin tritonus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τρίτονος (trítonos). By surface analysis, tri- + tone.
examples: The tritone has a pitch ratio close to 17:12.
The mini-epic “Seasons in the Abyss,” with its ringing tritone interval at the beginning, its extended solos, its medium tempo, was as close as Slayer got to a groove.

senses: The failure to make use of something.
ety: From non- + use.
examples: Sacred values, and the taboos that protect them, can be attached to resources that we decide are genuinely precious, such as identifiable lives, national borders, and the nonuse of chemical and nuclear weapons.

senses: A poet writing in Scots.
The national poet laureate of Scotland.
ety: From Scots makar. Doublet of maker.
examples: Could the role of makar, which at the least involves a creative interrogation of national identity, be filled by a poet who wasn’t a supporter of independence?

senses: The Jewish Diaspora (dispersion from Israel).
ety: Borrowed from Hebrew גָּלוּת (“exile”).
examples: Our forefathers, who fell away from serving the Almighty properly, caused its destruction and incurred the curse of galus.

senses: One who fakes something.
An impostor or impersonator.
A snake oil salesman; one who makes exaggerated claims about a product he sells.
ety: From fake + -er.
examples: The ordinary Christian will read the claims of the New Thought fakers with contempt; but have I not shown the Catholic Church publishing long lists of money-miracles?
All the doctor has to do nowadays is to read the labels on the bottles and boxes of samples the faker brings him.

senses: (Very) drunk or intoxicated.
ety: From blot + -o. The verb sense “to be annihilated or destroyed” may be related to blot out.
examples: Dear old Squiffy was always rather a lad for the wassail-bowl. When I met him in Paris, I remember, he was quite tolerably blotto.
I drank a lot of wine – and afterwards, at Les Vikings, Akvavit – and was completely blotto (well, not completely, but enough to talk a lot and get the Hungarian talking and not be bored).
I stayed home for a couple days and got blotto four times. I did the usual bad drunk routine; cried a lot, moaned about my life.

senses: To indulge in fantasy; to imagine things only possible in fantasy.
To portray in the mind, using fantasy.
ety: From fantasy + -ize.
examples: I fantasized about my ideal date.
Not that Mom and I didn't have our "shared experiences" — it's just that I'd like to forget most of them. I'd rather fantasize us together in that little cafe.
Actress Dana Delany fantasizes about making love with two men.

senses: A small Italian village.
ety: Borrowed from Italian borgo. Doublet of borough.
examples: The borgo’s five acres and five dilapidated structures were part of an estate once owned by the Borghese family, and overlooked a valley of hills and vineyards.

senses: A tropical evergreen shrub (Codiaeum variegatum), having glossy foliage, cultivated as a houseplant.
ety: From New Latin crotōn, from Ancient Greek κροτών (krotṓn, “tick”), from the size and shape of the seed.
examples: The croton bushes, by day hideous things like jaundiced laurels, were changed by the moon into jagged black and white designs like fantastic wood-cuts.

senses: A female hero.
ety: Blend of she + hero.
examples: Packing estrogen and, not infrequently, a pen and a sword, sheroes come in every imaginable shape, size, and color, and manifest their sheroism in infinite ways.

Every human grouping, whether it's just two people, a family, people in the neighborhood, people in the city, in a nation, a tribe, a species; people live in direct relation to the heroes and the sheroes they have.
He talks about how we must remember the unsung heroes and sheroes of the Talahassee boycott, of the movement in general, and finally, he wonders how C. K. Steele would be accepted here.

senses: Capable of stretching; elastic.
Inclined to stretch, as from weariness.
ety: From stretch + -y.
examples: Not just comfort, but luxurious comfort — the stretchy, yawny, sleepy kind — is his portion.

senses: The practice of proselytizing.
The state of being a proselyte.
ety: From proselyte + -ism.
examples: For quotations using this term, see Citations:proselytism.

senses: To mix or confuse.
To meet or unite in a confused way.
ety: From Middle English jumbelen, alteration of jumbren, jombren, a variant of jumpren, frequentative of jumpen (“to jump”), equal to jump + -le. More at jumber, jump, jumper.
examples: Every clime and age jumbled together.
I tried to study, but in my half-awake state, all of the concepts seemed to jumble together.

senses: A pair of tuned hand drums, used in various musical genres of the Indian subcontinent, that are similar to bongos.
ety: From Hindustani طبلہ / तबला (tablā), from Arabic طَبْلَة (ṭabla). Cognate of Catalan, Spanish, Portuguese tambor.
examples: Idealized membranes, plates and bars are clearly inadequate and give way to the reality of tablas, gongs and zanzas.

senses: A large wave, swell, surge, or undulating mass of something, such as water, smoke, fabric or sound.
ety: From Middle English *bilwe, borrowed from Old Norse bylgja, from Proto-Germanic *bulgijō. Cognates include Danish bølge (“wave”); Norwegian Bokmål bølge (“wave”), Norwegian Nynorsk bylgje (“wave”); Swedish bölja (“wave”); German Low German Bulge, Bulg, Bülg (“billow, wave”); German Bulge (“billow, wave”). Compare bellow, bawl.
examples: The snow fell hissing in the brine, / And the billows frothed like yeast.
The banners outflame the blazing morn, / O'er billows of bayonet, sword, and spear.
And the brooklet has found the billow / Though they flowed so far apart.

senses: Like a meteor in speed, brilliance, or ephemeralness.
Influenced by the weather.
ety: From meteor + -ic.
examples: Her meteoric rise to power was followed by a slow, lackluster career at the top.
With the meteoric rise has come broad concerns about the app’s impact on its relatively young users.
On the far side was reflected a single red and meteoric cloud, which had treasured one last crimson ray from the sunset, or perhaps nursed within it the fiery leaven.

senses: A loan or advance (of money)
A tax or duty
ety: From Middle English prest, from Old French prest, deverbal from prester.
examples: Requiring of the city a prest of six thousand marks.

senses: Resembling beads; small, round, and gleaming.
Bright and penetrating. (of eyes or a look)
Covered or ornamented with, or as if with, beads.
Characterized by beads.
ety: From bead + -y.
examples: I shivered in every limb, and a cold beady dew sprang out on my temples as I stood with eyes riveted on the spectral figure before me.
Cracked eggs, dead birds, scream as they fight for life / I can feel death, can see its beady eyes

senses: Causing much harm in a subtle way.
Causing death or injury; deadly.
Insidiously villainous: intending to cause harm, especially in a subtle way.
ety: From Middle English, from Old French pernicios, from Latin perniciōsus (“destructive”), from perniciēs (“destruction”), from per (“through”) + nex (“slaughter, death”).
examples: They warned of the pernicious effects of misinformation.
The weed has a pernicious influence on local crops.
Puritanism no longer employs the thumbscrew and lash; but it still has a most pernicious hold on the minds and feelings of the American people.

senses: A narrow passage or alley.
ety: Etymology unknown.
examples: He cut down a snicket between two houses, out into the fields.
Our bikes are where we left them at the entrance to an overgrown snicket of yew, ivy and Hart's-tongue fern, through which a stream dribbles its way into the Ouse.

senses: Bad-tempered, irritable, peevish, spiteful, habitually angry.
ety: The adjective form of spleen, borrowed from Late Latin spleneticus, from Latin splen. Anger was traditionally believed to originate from the fluids of the spleen.
examples: Horace seems to have purg'd himself from those Splenetick Reflections in those Odes and Epodes, before he undertook the Noble Work of Satires; which were properly so call'd.
In fact, Gwendolen, not intending it, but intending the contrary, had offended her hostess, who, though not a splenetic or vindictive woman, had her susceptibilities.

senses: A stream or pool in boggy land.
ety: From Middle English leche, for example Sandy's Letch located east of Annitsford in North Tyneside.
examples: The Letch near Killingworth Village flows in two branches: the Longbenton Letch and the Forest Hall Letch.

senses: To transport with joy or delight; to delight to ecstasy.
To have vigorous sexual intercourse with.
ety: From Middle English ravyschen, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French ravis-, present participle stem of ravir (“to seize; to take away hastily”), from Vulgar Latin *rapire, from Latin rapere. See also rape.
examples: That in things that do ravish with delight, men were not Masters of themselves, nor could they remember Gallateo's Rules; and that in time of Carnival, it was lawful to commit exorbitances.
Passepartout was ravished to behold this celebrated place, and thought that, with its circular walls and dismantled fort, it looked like an immense coffee-cup and saucer.

senses: Separated or disconnected; withdrawn; removed; apart.
Inattentive to surrounding objects; absent in mind; meditative.
ety: From abstract + -ed.
examples: I'm afraid neither of us was looking where we were going. We Adrians are notoriously abstracted, are we not?

senses: Very accurate in shooting or throwing.
Cold; unfriendly.
ety: From dead + eye. See glossary of nautical terms of "deadrise" for usage of "dead" to describe a stationary object or spatial stability of an object relative to motion. See nautical definition of "eye" for usage referring to the foremost part of a ship's bow that aims its orientation. For biological eye stabilization during head and neck movement, see vestibulo-ocular reflex
examples: Gross, only a 20-year-old junior, is a deadeye passer, a poised runner and a quick-thinking field general.
The old man was a natural sniper, a deadeye shooter even as a boy, and he served with my great uncle in the First World War.
The deadeye stare of the bassist was enough to make any normal person run.

senses: A long rattan cane used for corporal punishment.
ety: Borrowed from Malay rotan (“cane”), doublet of rattan.
examples: Two boys, aged 14 and 11, were each sentenced to three strokes of the light rotan at Kluang for stealing duck eggs from Loh Wee Seng.
Zaimi Bin Rassak, 20, was yesterday jailed for two years with two strokes of the rotan after he was found guilty of trafficking in 32 rolls of cannabis in Queens Crescent on June 24 at 1 a.m.
Khushwant Singh, 38-year-old on the run for five years, put behind bars for six years and two months; gets six strokes of the rotan.

senses: A protest in which a group of people surrounds a politician, building, etc. until demands are met.
ety: From Hindi घेराव (gherāv, “encirclement”).
examples: They had done a gherao and trapped the manager in his office for a whole day.
This was an invitation to strike: according to one estimate, there were more than 1,200 gheraos in the first six months of the first UF-LF government.

senses: The place on the diametrically opposite side of the earth from a given point.
The Southern Hemisphere.
The opposite of something.
ety: From Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀντίποδες (antípodes), from ἀντί (antí, “opposite”) + πόδες (pódes), plural of πούς (poús, “foot”).
examples: We should hold day with the Antipodes, If you would walk in absence of the sun.

The sleepy yet shrewd judge was the antipodes to confidence, but to Don Manuel he felt no hesitation in frankly stating his actions and their motives, from his first arrival in Spain to the present time.
The loud, rapid, eager tones, the incessant motion, the intense vital activity manifested in speech and action, are the very antipodes of the quiet, unimpulsive, unanimated Malay.

senses: One placed on watch, or in ambush.
A soldier sent on a forlorn hope.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French perdu, originally after sentinelle perdue.
examples: To watch, poor perdu, / With this thin helm?

senses: The basic, central, or main concept, drawing, or scheme of an architectural design.
Someone (especially a man) who is considered to be a good choice for marriage, because of wealth, status etc.
ety: From French parti.
examples: We met some time ago a man that would just do for you, if you were not already engaged to Jonathan. He is an excellent parti, being handsome, well off, and of good birth.

senses: A person, especially an entertainer, who practices ventriloquism.
ety: From ventriloquy + -ist.
examples: Most ridiculous is the discomfiture which attends the opponents of predication, who, like the ventriloquist Eurycles, have the voice that answers them in their own breast.

senses: An aging buffoon.
Trousers reminiscent of the tight-fitting leggings traditionally worn by a pantaloon.
A kind of fabric.
ety: Borrowed from French pantalon, from Italian Pantalone (a character in Commedia dell'arte), from Spanish Pantaleon (surname).
examples: The Bishop is a lean and slippered pantaloon, at least in his old clerical garments which he thinks good enough for the sea.

senses: A partitioned space for reading or studying, often in a library.
ety: A variant of carol (“small closet or enclosure”), from Middle English carole (“round dance with singing; group of people dancing and singing in a circle; circular thing; braid, chain (?); stall for study or writing; writing table; etc.”) (possibly referring to the fact that the item encloses or surrounds the person using it): see further at carol.
examples: He was busy writing his report in a small library carrel.
He then returned to his carrell for his own research.
Ah, the library. I booked like a madman for the Master’s Comp. Nine months, up in a study carrel on deck eight.

senses: A model of the shape of an object for purposes of collision detection.
ety: From collide + -er.
examples: The race controller will check for a trigger hit between this player's collider and the start/finish line trigger, but this script has an OnTriggerEnter function to check for triggers used to force a respawn.
